1.citation: Hervé-Fernández P, Houlbrèque F, Boisson F, Mulsow S, Teyssié JL, Oberhaënsli F, Azemard S, Jeffree R. Cadmium bioaccumulation and retention kinetics in the Chilean blue mussel Mytilus chilensis: seawater and food exposure pathways. Aquatic Toxicology. 2010;99(4):448–456. doi:10.1016/j.aquatox.2010.06.004. Explicit replacement for the unidentifiable Bao/cadmium-nanoparticle reference.
1.summary: This controlled radiotracer study followed cadmium uptake by Chilean blue mussels from seawater and algae, then measured elimination. The original abstract reports slower loss after seawater exposure than after dietary exposure.
1.establishes: Mussels can eliminate cadmium. Following seawater exposure, about 21% was lost over 52 days and the long-lived retention component had an estimated half-life above six months. About 20% of the food-derived tracer remained after ten days. These are experiment- and route-specific results, not proof of zero excretion, lifelong accumulation or a universal shellfish-to-fish ratio. Review was limited to the original abstract and bibliographic record.
1.relevance: It supports the revised article’s narrower claim that cadmium retention depends on exposure route. It does not support an oyster or clam mechanism, a filtration-rate generalization, an age effect or a certification threshold. The source was selected as a transparent replacement; the purported Bao study was not recovered.

4.referenceTitle: Contrasting trophic transfer patterns of cadmium and mercury in the Arctic marine food web of east Hudson Bay, Canada
4.citation: Rohonczy J, Chételat J, Robinson SA, et al. Contrasting trophic transfer patterns of cadmium and mercury in the Arctic marine food web of east Hudson Bay, Canada. Environmental Science and Pollution Research. 2024;31:20586–20600. Published 20 February 2024. doi:10.1007/s11356-024-32268-3.
4.summary: This 2014–2017 community-based Arctic study measured cadmium in 345 tissue samples. Blue-mussel soft tissue and urchin gonads were compared with fish, eider and seal tissues. Cadmium declined with trophic position in the muscle-based analysis; mercury increased.
4.establishes: Cadmium patterns depended strongly on tissue. High vertebrate liver burdens were interpreted as storage and detoxification. Concentrations were reported on a dry-weight basis; fish muscle was excluded from the cadmium model because many results were below detection.
4.relevance: The revised article uses this Arctic study to distinguish tissue, analyte and dry-weight reporting. It supplies no scallop or oyster distribution and cannot be treated as a wet-weight compliance survey or a universal bivalve-to-fish ratio.

6.referenceTitle: Maximum levels for cadmium in bivalve molluscs and cephalopods
6.citation: European Commission. Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006. OJ L119, 5 May 2023, pp. 103–157; entered into force 25 May 2023. Original text and consolidation dated 19 August 2026.
6.summary: Annex I sets wet-weight cadmium maxima of 1.0 mg/kg for bivalves and cephalopods without viscera, versus 0.050 mg/kg for fish muscle outside listed exceptions. For Pecten maximus, the bivalve maximum covers adductor muscle and gonad only.
6.establishes: These are binding food-category ceilings, not measured background distributions. Listed fish exceptions have higher limits. Article 3 addresses processing and concentration factors. The regulation does not establish cephalopod tissue concentration ranges or a unique biological explanation for each limit.
6.relevance: The article’s twentyfold comparison is between the 1.0 mg/kg bivalve cadmium ceiling and the 0.050 mg/kg default fish-muscle ceiling, not measured biological accumulation. HMTc must preserve the species exceptions, edible-tissue and wet-weight qualifications. The EU law does not itself validate HMTc’s ceiling or require its strictest-international-limit policy.
